Everyone should read classic Russian literature. You would imagine it to be dry and dull, and War and Peace is more often a "it's so long!" punchline than it is seriously recommended, but the characters written by Tolstoy and especially Dostoyevsky will seem alive and likely remind you of people you know, and they're so well rendered that you can put yourself into their frames of mind and understand even extraordinary decisions or experiences. Start with The Brothers Karamazov, in my opinion. Much like War and Peace, Crime and Punishment, or (with more social and pedestrian circumstances) Anna Karenina, it contains truths about the human condition and insights into love, hatred, death, happiness, joy, faith, despair, divorce, and what drives men to murder. You'll see through 19th century characters how our interactions with one another are more timeless than we imagine, and you'll see relationships and rivalries that are described with more clarity and insight than all modern novels that I know of.

It's more challenging, but there's also a novel called Demons (or The Possessed) by Dostoyevsky that predicts, with staggering foresight, both the mentality of the Russian Bolsheviks during the revolution and that of the modern Marxists and Communist-wannabies in the West. It follows a fictional revolutionary circle of young people who have rejected the more socially conservative values of their fathers in lieu of nihilism, which they use as a justification for ideological solipsism and acts of barbarity and murder. The self-congratulatory, atheistic, pseudo-intellectualism of Dostoyevsky's leftist revolutionaries is exactly what you could hear at a gathering of young Antifa Marxists when they hypocritically describe how "Nazis" need to be killed en masse in order to achieve peace and tolerance. How tolerance can be achieved through murder is a paradox that they always seem to be blind to. Ultimately their lofty revolutionary ideals for empowering the "noble, underprivileged, unfairly disadvantaged peasants" amount to nothing more than rioting, setting things on fire, and even murder--not to mention rejecting more traditional ideals as being inadequate while replacing them with degenerate behavior. You should also get a version that includes a censored chapter called "At Tikhon's," where one member of the circle recounts how he raped a 12 year old girl. I imagine all these things will sound familiar to Voat users.

Whether you go for the dense, character-dense political fare of Demons or the much more accessible The Brothers Karamazov, however, (which, by the way, has an ensemble of brothers that are similar to Arrested Development), you'll find that Russian literature isn't some inaccessible and boring relic of the past. It's actually more alive than much of what you can read today.

Both French and Russian literature are completely different from American literature, but I agree Russian literature in particular is of a very high quality. In American literature we are more used to realism over romanticism, and also action-packed conflict-driven plot-lines. Russian literature is much more focused on the characters and their relationships.
